title: Transports and the HTTP Header Contract

questions.question: A team debates whether Streamable HTTP and stdio need separate MCP message formats. What does the 2026-07-28 specification say?
options: Only Streamable HTTP requests carry a protocol version and capabilities; stdio requests do not.
Message semantics are identical everywhere; only framing and metadata delivery differ.
Each transport binding defines its own private set of methods and result types.
Streamable HTTP requires a newer JSON-RPC version than the stdio transport can use.
questions.explanation: Protocol semantics are identical on every transport; stdio and Streamable HTTP only differ in how messages are framed and how metadata like protocol version and capabilities is carried alongside them.

questions.question: A gateway forwards a tools/call request whose MCP-Protocol-Version header disagrees with the protocol version carried in the request body's _meta. What must the server do?
options: Reject it with HTTP 400 and a HeaderMismatch JSON-RPC error.
Trust the header value and continue processing the request normally.
Mint a fresh Mcp-Session-Id for the request and keep processing normally.
Reject it with an UnsupportedProtocolVersionError naming the versions it supports.
questions.explanation: The MCP-Protocol-Version header must equal the protocol version in the request body's _meta; when they disagree the server rejects the request with HTTP 400 and a HeaderMismatch (-32020) JSON-RPC error.

questions.question: A tool's inputSchema marks its region parameter with x-mcp-header set to Region, and the call argument for region is the plain ASCII value us-west1. What must the Mcp-Param-Region header contain?
options: The value base64 encoded, because every mirrored parameter header needs encoding.
Nothing at all, since x-mcp-header only ever applies to the Mcp-Name header.
The plain value us-west1, unchanged, since it needs no base64 sentinel encoding.
The value percent-encoded with URL escapes instead of the base64 sentinel format.
questions.explanation: Header values use the base64 sentinel format only when they cannot be safely represented as plain ASCII, such as non-ASCII characters, control characters, leading or trailing whitespace, or a value matching the sentinel pattern; a plain value like us-west1 is mirrored unchanged.

questions.question: A Streamable HTTP server receives a POST whose Origin header does not match any origin it allows. What does the specification require here?
options: Accept it anyway if the request also carries a valid bearer token.
Log the mismatch but continue processing the request as usual.
Respond 401 Unauthorized instead, since Origin is treated as authentication proof.
Respond 403 Forbidden, since this defends against DNS rebinding attacks.
questions.explanation: Streamable HTTP servers validate the Origin header on every connection to prevent DNS rebinding attacks and respond 403 Forbidden when it is present and not allowed; Origin validation is a defense in addition to authentication, not a substitute for it.

questions.question: A client sends an HTTP GET to the MCP endpoint, expecting the old standalone event stream to open. How does a modern 2026-07-28 server respond?
options: By opening an SSE stream and sending an endpoint event, as before.
By minting a fresh Mcp-Session-Id and starting a new session for it.
With 404 Not Found, since GET was never part of any MCP transport.
With 405 Method Not Allowed, since the modern endpoint only accepts POST.
questions.explanation: The 2026-07-28 Streamable HTTP transport removed the standalone GET stream and protocol sessions; a modern server answers GET or DELETE on the MCP endpoint with 405 Method Not Allowed instead of opening the deprecated HTTP+SSE event stream.

questions.question: Why does an accepted notification POST return 202 Accepted with no body, instead of a JSON-RPC result?
options: Because 202 itself carries a JSON-RPC result whose resultType is accepted.
Because a notification never gets a JSON-RPC reply; only its delivery is acknowledged.
Because notifications always fail validation, so the server returns nothing useful.
Because the client already learns the outcome from the Mcp-Method header alone.
questions.explanation: A notification has no id and never receives a JSON-RPC response; the transport instead acknowledges its delivery with HTTP 202 Accepted and no body, which is a transport-level outcome rather than a JSON-RPC result carrying a resultType.
